comparison: Perfect agreement on sediment characterization and microfluidic channel construction methodology (C1, C3, C10-C15, C68-C71). Both evaluations rate this as SUPPORTED with high praise for the μCT imaging approach and rigorous methodology.

Strong agreement on the main experimental finding of non-monotonic throughput behavior (C4, C20-C22). Both evaluations rate this as SUPPORTED and identify it as the key result with compelling evidence. Peer review R12 also addresses the control experiments (C18-C19) that OpenEval includes in this result.

Agreement on computational model validity (C5, C23). OpenEval provides detailed assessment of model parameterization and notes the limitation about slower sliding (C24-C29), while peer review focuses on the strength of coupling experiments with simulations and directly measured parameters (C38, C41). Peer R7 separately addresses the sliding behavior observations without criticism.

Agreement on the mechanistic explanation of trapping at high fields (C30-C36). Both evaluations rate this as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes quantitative reproduction across 10 geometries, while peer review explicitly acknowledges the trapping rationalization. Peer R5 separately addresses weak field behavior (C37), and peer R8 addresses C30 interpretation.

Agreement on UNCERTAIN status for the discrepancy at B=0 and its explanation (C42-C43). Both evaluations recognize this as a limitation. OpenEval notes the explanation is speculative without validation, while peer review identifies this as the main weakness regarding simulation-experiment comparison due to tracking limitations.

Perfect agreement on trap escape dynamics characterization (C44-C48). Both evaluations rate this as SUPPORTED. OpenEval provides detailed assessment of the Kramers escape analogy and statistical analysis, while peer review implicitly accepts this as part of the compelling theoretical framework.

Perfect agreement on experimental validation of trapping mechanism (C8, C50-C52). Both evaluations rate this as SUPPORTED and recognize the sequential field reduction experiment as clear confirmation of the simulation-predicted trapping effect.

Significant disagreement on evolutionary hypothesis (C6-C7, C9, C53-C56). OpenEval rates this as UNCERTAIN, noting the interpretation is speculative and requires further testing across species and evolutionary contexts. Peer review rates this as SUPPORTED, stating the authors 'provide strong arguments in favor of such a hypothesis' and explicitly endorsing the evolutionary adaptation claim.

Agreement on contextual claims about magnetotactic bacterial behavior (C57-C60). Both evaluations rate this as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes appropriate contextualization and logical distinctions, while peer review accepts these connections and suggests extending references without challenging the claims. Peer R13 also covers broader context (C61-C64).

Agreement on biological and physical context (C2, C61-C64). Both evaluations rate this as SUPPORTED. OpenEval emphasizes appropriate contextualization of habitat and magnetic field parameters, while peer review implicitly accepts these as part of the rigorous methodology. Peer R14 also covers bacterial culture details (C65-C67).

Agreement on bacterial culture and selection methodology (C65-C67). Both evaluations rate this as SUPPORTED. OpenEval notes clear methodological details important for reproducibility, while peer review praises the careful methodology without questioning these details.

Agreement on control experiments (C18-C19). Both evaluations rate this as SUPPORTED. OpenEval includes these controls as part of demonstrating the key experimental finding, while peer review separately acknowledges them as important validation that the effect is specific to obstacle geometry.
